extracted.intended_audience: researchers, policymakers, journalists, and the public interested in FCC public comments and net neutrality policy
extracted.subtask_description: Assessment and quantitative analysis of the 21.7 million public comments submitted to the FCC during the 2017 net neutrality comment period, focusing on data quality, duplication, automation, and evidence of organized campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Many submissions seemed to include false or misleading personal information
rubrics_metrics.description: The Center’s analysis finds evidence that many people did not reveal their true identities when submitting comments to the FCC; some instances may be accidental, but patterns indicate intentional entry of false or misleading personal information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators include repeated author names (e.g., 'Net Neutrality', 'The Internet'), widely repeated or nonfunctional email addresses, and use of disposable/temporary emails. Examples: 'Net Neutrality' appeared ~17,000 times, 'The Internet' ~7,500 times. Investigate author-name repetition, non-name authors, and cross-check email validity when assessing identity claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of temporary or duplicate email addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Some 57% of the comments utilized either duplicate email addresses or temporary email addresses designed to be used briefly and then discarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the share of comments tied to duplicate emails and to known disposable-email-provider domains. The report identified 1.4 million email addresses that appeared multiple times, and more than 8 million submissions included email addresses from temporary email accounts. Report both absolute counts and percentages when evaluating dataset reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Email addresses missing required format or missing entirely
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances where the supplied email did not contain the '@' character or where an email address was not provided at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this dataset, 9,190 comments had email addresses without an '@' and 10% of comments contained no email address. Flag and quantify malformed or missing contact information as a data-quality metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconsistent use of FCC email verification process
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the FCC submission form indicated an email validation step, the site did not appear to use this process consistently; only 3% of the comments definitively went through validation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for evidence of verification (e.g., verification tokens, bounce records). When the platform's verification is inconsistent, treat self-reported contact information as less reliable and document verification rates in reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplicate and highly similar comment submissions (bulk/templated messages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the 21.7 million comments posted, 6% were unique and 94% were submitted multiple times; many comments are exact duplicates or near-duplicates, and a small set of popular messages account for a large share of submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify uniqueness vs duplication. In this case five comments were submitted >800,000 times, seven most-submitted comments comprised 38% of all submissions. Use textual-similarity grouping (see similarity threshold) and count exact-duplicate occurrences and near-duplicate clusters to assess how many independent voices are actually present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual similarity grouping threshold (cosine similarity >= .95)
rubrics_metrics.description: The analysis used cosine similarity measured on character sequences; comments with cosine similarity of at least .95 (scale 0-1) were grouped together and considered the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify and justify the similarity threshold used to collapse near-duplicates. The report used .95; document the algorithm, parameterization (character-level cosine), and how grouping affects uniqueness counts. Provide sensitivity checks with other thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneous-submission timestamp spikes as indicator of automated/bulk filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Many instances where thousands (and in some cases hundreds of thousands) of comments were submitted at the exact same second — a signature consistent with automated or bulk submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze precise timestamps to detect submissions that share identical second-level timestamps. Report counts of events exceeding thresholds (e.g., >25,000 same-second submissions, >75,000 same-second submissions). Examples: 9 occasions had >75,000 at the same second; one example had 475,482 submissions at 2:57:15 p.m. EDT on July 19.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patterns of variation within mass-submitted comments (identical vs minor variations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass-submitted comments sometimes were entirely identical; other times they showed minor, systematic variations (e.g., different 'signed' names or template openings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish exact duplicates from templated variants. For templated variants, identify which fields vary (name, greeting, a phrase) and whether variation is systematic (e.g., same core body, different author names). Use this to infer submission mechanism (automated script with name list vs manual copying).

rubrics_metrics.name: Traceability of comment text to external websites/organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Text of many of the top comments can be traced back to a small number of organizations or webpages (e.g., battleforthenet.com, Taxpayers Protection Alliance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match comment text to content published on external sites to attribute organized campaigns. Quantify how many submissions correspond to each source and report share of total comments traceable to specific external campaigns or platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Off-topic and nonsensical comments present in the dataset
rubrics_metrics.description: Some comments had nothing to do with net neutrality (e.g., Bee Movie script excerpts, strings with more non-alphanumeric than alphanumeric characters, short meaningless messages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify and count clearly off-topic or spammy comments. Examples in this dataset: at least 34 comments referenced Bee Movie; 108 comments had more non-alphanumeric than alphanumeric characters; many consisted of one-word or punctuation-only posts. Report how off-topic content affects the effective sample of substantive comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burstiness and correlation with external events
rubrics_metrics.description: The comment period featured long stretches with few submissions punctuated by bursts of intense activity correlated with external events (e.g., John Oliver segment, FCC DDoS news release, 'Day of Action').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze temporal patterns (daily and event-window counts) and correlate spikes with external triggers. Example: more than 2.1 million comments were submitted in the five days after May 7 events; July 12 ('Day of Action') produced 1.4 million comments in one day. Use event-linked analysis to interpret causation vs baseline activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive proportion and count metrics for dataset characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting counts and percentages of key phenomena (e.g., 21.7 million total comments, 6% unique, 57% duplicate/temp-email, share of top comments) to summarize dataset reliability and composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide absolute counts and relative proportions for transparency. Include counts for unique comments, duplicates, top-N most-submitted messages, temporary-email occurrences, malformed emails, and verified-email rate. Use these descriptive statistics to contextualize claims about public sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data provenance and reproducibility (use of FCC API and methodology transparency)
rubrics_metrics.description: All comments were downloaded via the FCC’s publicly available API; data and comments used in the report are stored on the FCC site and are freely available. The report documents methods (cosine similarity, domain matching) in the methodology section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing public-comment datasets, document data source, extraction method (API endpoints, timestamps), preprocessing steps, similarity and domain-matching algorithms, and limitations. Make code and replication files available when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for identifying disposable or temporary email addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Disposable email addresses were identified by matching comment email domains to a list of known providers of temporary/disposable email accounts; some services use random domains that cannot be tracked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain and disclose the list of disposable-email domains used for matching (report included examples: @pornhub.com and 10 domains from FakeMailGenerator.com like @gustr.com and @armyspy.com). Note limitations: services that use random domains (e.g., 10minutemail.com) may evade detection, so disposable-email counts are conservative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive caution: bulk filing is not inherently illegitimate
rubrics_metrics.description: The report notes that bulk filing or simultaneously submitted comments are not inherently wrong or sinister; a third party might repost text, or organized campaigns may be legitimate advocacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing organized or automated behavior, include contextual interpretation and do not assume malevolent intent. Distinguish between methodological detection (duplicates, timestamps) and normative judgments about legitimacy; recommend documenting provenance before drawing policy conclusions.
